item.title: Jumio rolls out selfie-first reusable identity across APAC
item.dc:creator: TNGlobal
item.description: Jumio has expanded selfie.DONE across Asia-Pacific, offering previously verified users a selfie-first path through identity checks while retaining risk controls.
item.content:encoded:
Identity-verification company Jumio has expanded its selfie-first reusable identity product, selfie.DONE, across Asia-Pacific, extending a rollout that previously covered Latin America and North America.

The product allows previously enrolled and trusted users to begin verification with a selfie rather than resubmitting an identity document for every new onboarding flow. Jumio said higher-risk or unrecognized users can still be routed through full document verification.

Reusable identity moves into APAC onboarding

Jumio said selfie.DONE relies on a consented global identity graph that can recognize previously verified users across participating customer environments. The company positions the approach as a way to reduce repeated identity-document checks while keeping risk assessment active during each interaction.

The APAC rollout targets regulated and high-friction onboarding use cases in financial services, crypto, gaming and sharing-economy platforms.

Jumio said deployments of the product have produced a 20 percent increase in verification completion rates, with up to 60 percent of users completing document-free selfie verification. Those figures are company-reported results and were not broken out specifically for Asia-Pacific in the announcement.

Identity graph supports cross-customer recognition

The company said its identity graph contains more than 75 million legitimate and fraudulent identities and is growing by around 85,000 identities per day. Jumio uses that data to compare a new verification attempt with previously observed identities and risk signals.

Bala Kumar, president and chief product and technology officer at Jumio, said mobile-first markets in Asia-Pacific create demand for faster onboarding while regulated businesses still need strong assurance and compliance controls.

The model reflects a broader shift from one-time identity checks toward continuous identity and risk assessment. TNGlobal recently reported on how fraud and anti-money-laundering providers are expanding across the Philippines and Southeast Asia as digital transactions create new verification and monitoring demands.

Malaysia fintech watches the rollout

The announcement also included comments from Nimbura, a Malaysia-based financial-technology platform that connects consumers with digital lending and financing services.

Artjoms Borcovs, CEO for Asia at Nimbura, said selfie-first verification could reduce onboarding friction for trusted customers if security and compliance are maintained. The announcement describes Nimbura as monitoring the expansion and evaluating its potential. It does not identify the company as a confirmed selfie.DONE customer or deployment.

That distinction is relevant because reusable identity networks depend on both user consent and sufficient ecosystem participation. A faster onboarding experience can be attractive to digital lenders and other regulated services, but adoption will also depend on how local privacy, identity and financial rules apply to the reuse of verification data across markets.

Jumio said it has processed more than one billion identity-related transactions across more than 200 countries and territories. The company did not disclose APAC-specific customer numbers for selfie.DONE in the supplied announcement.

item.title: Flam raises $40 million Series B for interactive AI content
item.dc:creator: TNGlobal
item.description: Flam raised $40 million in a QED Investors-led Series B to develop interactive AI content tools and expand enterprise sales, with activity in India and Southeast Asia.
item.content:encoded:
Flam has raised $40 million in a Series B round led by QED Investors to develop its interactive AI content products and expand enterprise sales. The company said in its September 15 announcement that existing investors RTP Global and Dovetail participated again, alongside Claypond Capital and several individual backers.

The San Francisco and Bengaluru-based company builds tools for interactive video, 3D product experiences and conversational visual agents. Moneycontrol reported the financing and identified Flam’s Bengaluru operations and Indian founders. The company did not disclose a valuation or the stakes acquired by investors.

Flam said the new capital will fund research and development on its AI models, an expanded product suite and sales growth in international markets. It also said it had signed more than 100 enterprise customers over six quarters. The customer figure was supplied by Flam and was not independently audited in the material reviewed.

Products and regional activity

Flam’s Flicks format lets viewers switch a person, product or scene during video playback. Its Airboards format streams 3D content to a camera interface, where users can interact through touch and voice. The company’s Visual Agents are designed as on-screen characters that can conduct conversations and carry out actions. Those descriptions reflect Flam’s own product account; the release does not establish how widely each format has been deployed.

The company has also described AI models for editing image elements, generating video assets, facial motion, speech and language responses. Its release lists performance figures for streaming and response times, but does not provide independent testing or a common benchmark. Flam’s products target marketing, product visualization, customer support and sales, among other enterprise uses.

Flam said it has partnered with Indonesia’s Elang Mahkota Teknologi, or Emtek, to bring its technology to brands in Southeast Asia. The announcement did not disclose commercial terms, customer rollouts or an implementation schedule for that partnership. Flam named Grab among its enterprise customers, but did not provide details of the work undertaken for the Singapore-based company.

Funding context

QED Investors co-founder Nigel Morris and partner Sandeep Patil were quoted in the issuer’s release discussing Flam’s technology and customer traction. Their comments support the investor’s involvement but are not an independent assessment of the company’s sales or product performance.

Moneycontrol said Flam previously raised a $14 million Series A led by RTP Global in May 2025. It reported that the startup was founded in 2021 by Shourya Agarwal, Malhar Patil and Amit Gaiki. SiliconANGLE also covered the Series B and the company’s focus on interactive videos and 3D experiences. Some investor and customer names differ among published accounts; this article follows the issuer’s release for the new round and leaves disputed additions out.

The financing comes as companies test AI-generated material for advertising and commerce. Flam’s announcement, however, did not disclose revenue, profitability, the number of active customers or how much of its business comes from Southeast Asia. Those measures remain important for judging whether its tools move beyond demonstrations into recurring use.

item.title: Japan’s Ricoh invests in Singapore mental-health platform Intellect via $20M venture fund
item.dc:creator: Duc Dao
item.description: Japan's Ricoh has invested in Intellect, a Singapore-based workplace mental-health platform, through its corporate venture-capital fund, in the fund's first deal.
item.content:encoded:
Japan’s Ricoh has invested in Intellect, a Singapore-based workplace mental-health platform, through its corporate venture-capital fund, in the fund’s first deal.

In a statement on Tuesday, Ricoh said the investment was made through the RICOH Innovation Fund II, a JPY3 billion yen ($20 million) fund launched in April. SBI Investment is a general partner. Ricoh said the fund targeted areas including workplace creativity, digital work, and digital inclusion.

Ricoh did not provide any financial details.

Employee well-being is a foundation for creativity and productivity, Ricoh noted. The Japanese firm will explore combining Intellect’s mental-health expertise with data from its own workplace-services business.

Intellect provides organizations with mental-health support spanning self-care, coaching, counseling and workforce analytics, with a dashboard for tracking employee well-being. Its services are available in more than 100 countries and over 120 languages, serving more than 4 million users.

Eiji Suzuki, a general manager in Ricoh’s corporate-planning division, said Intellect’s platform and data capabilities made it a compelling partner. Theodoric Chew, Intellect’s co-founder and chief executive, said Ricoh’s workplace expertise would help extend mental healthcare to more organizations.

Founded in 2019 by Theodoric Chew, Intellect has raised over $22 million to date from investors including Tiger Global, Y Combinator, Insignia Ventures Partners, and the hospital group IHH Healthcare, a strategic backer.

item.title: China’s AlphaPai raises $50M Series B for AI investment-research assistant
item.dc:creator: Duc Dao
item.description: China's AlphaPai, an AI assistant for investment research, has raised $50 million in a Series B round backed by major Chinese financial institutions, its third funding round in a year.
item.content:encoded:
China’s AlphaPai, an AI assistant for investment research, has raised $50 million in a Series B round backed by major Chinese financial institutions, its third funding round in a year.

In a statement on Tuesday, AlphaPai said the round drew strategic investors from across finance, including China Insurance Investment, the national investment platform for the country’s insurance industry, and GF Xinde Investment Management, the private-equity arm of GF Securities. Qiming Venture Partners, Ambrum Capital, Next Capital, Trustar Capital, and Eastern Bell Capital also took part, with China Renaissance as financial adviser.

AlphaPai, developed by Shanghai-based Rabyte Technology, provides AI tools for professional investors, moving from meeting summaries into core investment research and analysis. It serves more than 120,000 professional users across over 8,000 financial institutions and asset managers.

In April, the company launched PaiWork, an AI investment-research workstation combining financial data, research tools and AI agents in one workspace. It has since added a benchmark for testing AI on research tasks and a partner program with more than 40 brokerage research units and data providers.

AlphaPai will utilize the proceeds to increase research-and-development spending, expand its client base across asset classes, and grow abroad while deepening its home market. The Series B follows a pre-Series A of $14 million in October 2025 and a Series A of $28 million in March 2026.

Founder and Chief Executive Luodan Li said building financial AI was a long-term, systematic effort, and that the company aimed to bring its technology to the core of global finance.

item.title: Dutch chip-security firm Fortaegis raises $50M Series A led by Singapore-based Serendipity Capital
item.dc:creator: Duc Dao
item.description: Dutch chip-security startup Fortaegis Technologies has raised $50 million in an oversubscribed Series A round led by Singapore-based Serendipity Capital, to move its silicon-based "Secure Compute" technology into commercial production.
item.content:encoded:
Dutch chip-security startup Fortaegis Technologies has raised $50 million in an oversubscribed Series A round led by Singapore-based Serendipity Capital, to move its silicon-based “Secure Compute” technology into commercial production.

In a statement last Sunday, Amsterdam-based Fortaegis said it would utilize the money to scale production of its programmable-chip products across the United States, Europe, Singapore, and Japan. It will also advance a roadmap toward custom-designed chips, while enlarging its engineering and commercial teams.

The round was led by returning investor Serendipity Capital and included TEL Venture Capital, the venture arm of Japanese chip-equipment maker Tokyo Electron, the Dutch research organisation TNO, and Prodrive Technologies, along with several smaller funds. Individual backers included Ilyas Khan, founder of quantum-computing firm Quantinuum and Fortaegis’s chairman, and Chris Miller, a board member and author of “Chip War.”

Fortaegis builds security into the chip itself, generating encryption keys from the tiny physical variations each silicon chip acquires during manufacturing. The keys change constantly and are not permanently stored, an approach can make them harder to steal and more resistant to future quantum-computer attacks.

Fortaegis said its architecture was quantum-safe by design and had shown connection speeds more than 200 times faster than conventional methods in internal and customer testing.

Fortaegis’s technology can help AI infrastructure, defence and autonomous systems, telecommunications, critical infrastructure and, automotive.

Chief Executive Boudewijn Wijnands said security could no longer be added on top of digital systems but had to be built into the foundations of computing. Rob Jesudason, Serendipity Capital’s chief executive, said demand for hardware-embedded security would grow as AI and quantum computing scaled.

item.title: Google Cloud opens Singapore Engineering Center to build AI and cloud products for global markets
item.dc:creator: TNGlobal
item.description: Google Cloud has opened a Singapore Engineering Center linking AI research, cloud product development and enterprise deployment across Southeast Asia.
item.content:encoded:
Google Cloud has opened its Singapore Engineering Center, a product development hub intended to turn AI and cloud research into production systems for enterprises in Singapore and other global markets.

The center brings together engineers working across AI, AI infrastructure, data, compute, machine learning, core networking, storage and customer-facing engineering. It is co-located with Google DeepMind’s Southeast Asia research presence, giving Google a Singapore base that links research, product engineering and customer deployment.

Google Cloud said the Singapore Engineering Center will work directly with enterprises on systems designed for agentic workloads, localized AI applications, developer tooling and hybrid or multicloud environments. The company first announced plans for the center in February 2026.

Singapore hub links research with enterprise deployment

Supported by Singapore’s Economic Development Board, the center has three broad areas of work. These include infrastructure for low-latency and mission-critical agentic workloads, the integration of foundation-model capabilities into enterprise systems, and developer platforms that can automate more of the software delivery process.

Google Cloud said the model differs from a conventional regional support office because engineers in Singapore will contribute to products intended for wider deployment. The company is also expanding its regional Forward Deployed Engineer workforce, which works with customers to move tailored systems from pilots into production.

Beng Kong Pee, executive vice president of the Singapore Economic Development Board, said the center would add engineering depth to the country’s AI and cloud ecosystem and create opportunities for Singapore-based engineers to work with frontier technologies.

Grab and DBS among early collaborators

Google Cloud cited Grab and DBS as early examples of customer collaboration linked to the Singapore engineering operation. Work with Grab has included stress-testing real-time multilingual AI models, while DBS has been involved in work around financial agentic workflows.

DBS Chief Transformation and Data Officer Nimish Panchmatia said the bank sees Singapore as having an opportunity to develop as a trusted global AI hub. DBS has been advancing an agentic AI strategy and said it expects continued industry collaboration around safe and responsible deployment.

The new center also adds to a broader push to build AI infrastructure and engineering capacity in Southeast Asia. TNGlobal has previously examined how the region is trying to strengthen resilient digital infrastructure for AI adoption, including the need to balance compute growth with reliability, security and sovereignty requirements.

Product development moves closer to regional customers

Moe Abdula, vice president of Customer Engineering for Asia Pacific at Google Cloud, said Singapore was chosen because building for the diversity of Asia Pacific can expose engineering teams to a wide range of deployment requirements.

The center gives Google Cloud a place to bring research, core product development and implementation teams into a shorter feedback loop with customers. For enterprises, the practical test will be whether this reduces the time between an AI pilot and a system that can operate reliably at production scale.

Google Cloud did not disclose the number of engineers assigned to the center or a specific investment figure in the material supplied to TNGlobal.

item.title: TrueMoney taps Fireblocks for Thailand blockchain-payment pilot
item.dc:creator: TNGlobal
item.description: TrueMoney is using Fireblocks embedded-wallet infrastructure for THBT Phase 2, a Thailand blockchain-payment pilot operating within regulatory sandboxes.
item.content:encoded:
Thailand’s TrueMoney has partnered with digital asset infrastructure company Fireblocks to power the embedded wallet layer for the second phase of Thai Baht TrueMoney, or THBT, a blockchain-based payment pilot.

TrueMoney said THBT is a Thai baht-referenced digital value unit being tested under the Bank of Thailand’s Enhanced Regulatory Sandbox. The second phase places a Fireblocks-powered wallet directly inside the TrueMoney application so users do not have to manage private keys through a separate self-custody wallet.

Thailand pilot targets everyday payment use cases

The companies said eligible participants can use THBT to purchase digital coupons through the THBTStore or exchange it with six supported digital assets. Those exchange services are operated by Ascend Bit under the Thai Securities and Exchange Commission’s Digital Asset Regulatory Sandbox, according to the announcement.

The setup also targets international users. Tourists and expatriates holding supported digital assets can swap them for THBT, use the balance for eligible purchases or withdraw THBT into Thai baht through the participating ecosystem.

TrueMoney said applications for Phase 2 will remain open through December 31, 2026, with the pilot capped at as many as 20,000 Thai and international participants.

Embedded wallets hide more of the Web3 complexity

The Fireblocks integration is designed to handle wallet creation, security and assisted recovery inside the TrueMoney experience. That approach removes the need for mainstream users to handle a seed phrase or private key directly.

Apinand Dabpetch, managing director of Ascend Bit and group head of Wallet & Growth at TrueMoney, said the project is intended to make digital assets easier to use while retaining security and regulatory controls.

Ran Goldi, senior vice president of Payments and Network at Fireblocks, said the goal is for the blockchain infrastructure to sit behind the payment experience rather than require users to understand Web3 mechanics.

Regulated pilots are becoming a path to payment experiments

The THBT project adds another example of payment companies in Southeast Asia testing new settlement and wallet models inside regulatory sandboxes rather than launching them as unrestricted consumer products.

That distinction is important because the pilot remains bounded by participation limits, supported assets and sandbox rules. It should therefore be viewed as a regulated test of programmable payments and embedded-wallet design rather than a general replacement for Thai baht payment systems.

TrueMoney, part of Ascend Money, operates financial services in several Southeast Asian markets, including Thailand, Cambodia, Myanmar, Vietnam, the Philippines, Indonesia and Malaysia.

The launch also fits a broader regional push to make digital payment infrastructure easier to use across borders. TNGlobal recently covered how cross-border QR payment initiatives are expanding in the Philippines and Southeast Asia, although the THBT pilot uses a different blockchain-based architecture.

item.title: Southeast Asia leads SAS trustworthy AI index, but ROI and audit rates slip
item.dc:creator: TNGlobal
item.description: A SAS and IDC study finds stronger trustworthy-AI scores across Singapore, Malaysia and Thailand, even as reported ROI and regular audit rates decline.
item.content:encoded:
Southeast Asian organizations scored above the global benchmark across all five dimensions of a SAS trustworthy-AI index in 2026, but the same regional study found that reported returns and regular AI audits weakened even as adoption accelerated.

The findings come from SAS’s second annual Data and AI Impact Report, which incorporates research from IDC. The global study surveyed 2,699 decision-makers across 28 countries. Its Southeast Asia results are a sample-weighted composite of Singapore, Malaysia and Thailand, based on 122 respondents in 2026, compared with 120 in 2025.

Trustworthiness scores rise across the regional sample

SAS said Southeast Asia’s Trustworthiness Index rose from 57.7 in 2025 to 66.5 in 2026. The gap between perceived trust and measured trustworthiness narrowed from 14.6 points to 6.6 points.

The region improved across each of the study’s five dimensions. Data quality and governance reached 66.7, model governance and oversight 64.2, explainability and fairness 63.7, responsible AI policy 71.2, and audit and accountability 70.5.

SAS said Southeast Asia was the only market grouping in the study to outperform the global benchmark across all five dimensions. Because the regional sample covers Singapore, Malaysia and Thailand rather than every ASEAN economy, the result should be read as a three-market composite rather than a measure of the entire region.

AI maturity is rising faster than infrastructure

The report found a widening gap between AI ambition and infrastructure readiness. Advanced AI maturity in the Southeast Asian sample rose by 20.5 points, while infrastructure maturity increased by 4.1 points.

Spending intentions are still rising. Around 65.6 percent of respondents planned a small increase in AI spending over the next 12 months, while 14.8 percent planned a large increase.

That creates pressure on organizations to strengthen the data, compute and governance systems underneath more autonomous AI. TNGlobal has previously reported how organizations in the region are trying to balance AI adoption with explainability and the ability to prove how AI decisions are made.

Higher trust scores have not yet produced higher returns

The regional Impact Index remained almost flat, slipping from 58.3 to 58.0. The share of organizations reporting strong or high return on AI investment fell from 36.7 percent to 28.7 percent.

The study also found that employees were still overriding AI recommendations when systems could not provide enough context. Insufficient explanation was cited by 37.8 percent of respondents, while 37 percent pointed to a lack of situational context.

Deepak Ramanathan, vice president of Customer Advisory at SAS, said the next challenge for organizations in Southeast Asia is converting stronger trustworthiness into measurable business results while maintaining explainability and control as autonomous systems expand.

Audit frequency falls despite governance gains

One of the report’s more cautionary findings concerns verification. Although the Audit & Accountability score rose by 11.3 points to 70.5, the proportion of organizations conducting regular AI audits or impact assessments fell from 47.3 percent to 21.3 percent.

That decline suggests formal governance frameworks may be improving faster than recurring operational checks. As organizations deploy more agentic systems, the difference could become more important because autonomous workflows can make decisions or take actions with less direct human intervention.

Chris Marshall, vice president at IDC, said stronger oversight, explainability, accountability and data foundations are becoming prerequisites for scaling AI successfully.

The study covers banking, insurance, life sciences and the public sector. Its regional findings offer a useful snapshot of Singapore, Malaysia and Thailand, but the relatively small Southeast Asian sample means year-on-year shifts should be interpreted with care.

item.title: China’s Tencent Cloud, Malaysia’s U Mobile to cooperate in enterprise 5G, AI
item.dc:creator: Duc Dao
item.description: Tencent Cloud, the cloud unit of Chinese technology giant Tencent, and Malaysia's U Mobile will jointly develop 5G and AI solutions for businesses in Malaysia, the companies said.
item.content:encoded:
Tencent Cloud, the cloud unit of Chinese technology giant Tencent, and Malaysia’s U Mobile will jointly develop 5G and AI solutions for businesses in Malaysia, the companies said.

In a statement on Monday, Tencent Cloud said the two sides have signed a memorandum of understanding for the move. Tencent Cloud will combine its AI and cloud services with U Mobile’s 5G network and its Enterprise Innovation Platform to develop, test, and demonstrate applications for enterprises and smaller firms.

Successful cases can advance to pilot deployments and commercial launch. No financial terms were disclosed.

U Mobile, Malaysia’s newest 5G network operator, launched its ULTRA5G service in 2025 and opened the enterprise platform this year as a testing ground for 5G and AI projects. Tencent Cloud said the deal was its first AI-focused partnership with a Malaysian telecommunications company.

Poshu Yeung, a senior vice president at Tencent Cloud and head of its international business, said the partnership can help enterprises and developers build 5G and AI applications supporting Malaysia’s digital transformation. Woon Ooi Yuen, U Mobile’s chief technology officer, said the tie-up can turn ideas into practical solutions through the platform’s develop-test-demonstrate approach.

The companies said they would run workshops, demonstrations, and pilot showcases with businesses, startups, developers and universities, and share expertise in areas such as 5G, AI, system integration, and security.

item.title: SES completes O3b mPOWER constellation after final launch
item.dc:creator: TNGlobal
item.description: SES launched the final three O3b mPOWER satellites, completing its 13-spacecraft MEO constellation ahead of their planned mid-2027 service entry.
item.content:encoded:
SES has launched the final three satellites for its O3b mPOWER network, completing the 13-spacecraft medium Earth orbit constellation. The new satellites are expected to enter service by mid-2027 after orbit raising, testing and commissioning.

The O3b mPOWER 11, 12 and 13 satellites lifted off on a SpaceX Falcon 9 from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida at 2:49 p.m. local time on September 13, according to SES. Spaceflight Now independently confirmed the launch and deployment sequence.

Ten O3b mPOWER satellites are already operating. SES said the three additions will increase capacity and resilience for enterprise, government, mobility and telecommunications customers, particularly in remote or difficult-to-serve locations.

Service expansion follows commissioning

The launch completed the spacecraft deployment phase, but the latest satellites are not yet carrying commercial traffic. They must reach their operating orbits and pass technical checks before entering service, a process SES expects to finish around the middle of 2027.

SES said its operational O3b mPOWER network can provide capacity ranging from tens of megabits per second to several gigabits per second for an individual site. Actual service levels depend on customer contracts, terminals, location and network configuration.

The constellation uses software-defined Boeing 702X satellites in medium Earth orbit. Compared with geostationary satellites, the lower orbit can reduce signal travel time. SES markets the system for mobile backhaul, cloud access, maritime and aviation connectivity, remote industrial sites and government communications.

Boeing built the spacecraft, while SpaceX launched all 13 satellites across six Falcon 9 missions beginning in December 2022. Commercial service started in April 2024 with the first six satellites.

Design changes expanded the constellation

SES originally planned an 11-satellite system. The company disclosed in its 2023 results that power-module issues affecting the first four spacecraft could reduce available capacity and operating life. It upgraded satellites seven through 11 and added satellites 12 and 13 within its existing capital expenditure plan.

Spaceflight Now reported that the design changes were introduced before later spacecraft were completed. The publication said the additional satellites were intended to offset the effects of the early electrical issue and strengthen the overall network.

The three new spacecraft bring the constellation to the revised total of 13. SES cautioned that expected capacity, performance and availability remain subject to launch, commissioning and operational risks.

Asia-Pacific service footprint

O3b mPOWER is a global network with existing use in Asia-Pacific. In February 2025, Via Satellite reported that Viasat Energy Services had deployed O3b mPOWER capacity on an offshore production vessel in the region. The service supports operational and crew communications aboard the vessel.

The system has also been linked to connectivity projects serving India, Australia, New Zealand and Pacific markets. The September 13 announcement did not identify new Asia-Pacific customers or allocate a specific share of the added capacity to the region.

SES completed its acquisition of Intelsat in 2025, combining geostationary and medium Earth orbit assets under one operator. The company is developing a broader multi-orbit network strategy, with O3b mPOWER positioned as its high-throughput MEO layer.

Customer access to the final three satellites will begin only after commissioning. SES has not disclosed a more precise in-service date or regional activation schedule.
